fit: neuropathology with exclusions for established Parkinson motor onset
assessment: The clinicopathologic comparison includes 106 autopsy-confirmed dementia cases, 89 with Alzheimer pathology alone and 17 with Lewy body variant. It excludes Parkinson motor onset more than 12 months before dementia. Visual hallucination history predicted Lewy body pathology in the fitted model (OR 7.3, 95% CI 1.71–31.08). The model predicts neuropathology from a clinical feature and provides no fig exposure or exposure-linked episode rate.

fit: formed visual hallucination history in low vision
assessment: A low-vision rehabilitation cohort asked 225 first-time referrals about formed visual hallucinations. Seventy-eight (35%) reported them. Worse measured contrast sensitivity retained an association after adjustment for acuity and other covariates. The outcome is presence in a vision-clinic population. The study does not compare fig intake or Parkinson episode rates.

fit: one-month Parkinson interviews by hallucination modality
assessment: Structured interviews of 116 consecutive Parkinson outpatients covered the preceding month. The authors report 42% with hallucinations in any modality, including 16% visual and 35% nonvisual with overlap. These are proportions of patients, and neither dried fig intake nor a food-linked change in episode frequency was measured.

fit: retrospective Parkinson hallucination groups and regional structure
assessment: The retrospective structural MRI included 13 non-demented Parkinson patients with visual hallucinations and 16 without, plus 13 Parkinson dementia cases with hallucinations and 11 dementia with Lewy bodies cases. The non-demented Parkinson contrast found a pedunculopontine-region gray matter difference. The thalamic difference appeared in the combined comparison with dementia included. The exposure was clinical group status and the result was structural imaging.

fit: stimulus-evoked images and a separate Lewy body patient score
assessment: Cortical stimulation in 21 dementia with Lewy bodies patients and 19 controls found no overall group difference in phosphene threshold or response rate. Within patients both measures correlated with the past-month hallucination frequency-by-severity score. Six patients and no controls reported transient complex images during stimulation. This study does not measure a dried fig effect or spontaneous Parkinson episode rates.

fit: dementia group connectivity with visual diagnostic criteria
assessment: Resting-state imaging compared dementia with Lewy bodies, Alzheimer dementia and healthy controls. Visual hallucinations were among the core features used to classify the Lewy body cases. The analysis mapped connectivity between selected brain regions and did not assign or measure a fig exposure or its association with repeated visual episodes.

fit: Parkinson hallucination history and sleep related falling
assessment: Thirteen of 50 Parkinson patients reported sleep-related falling out of bed. The original reports more people with a history of visual hallucinations among those who fell. Five fallers with hallucinations had used quetiapine, and the groups differed in some medication use. This is a patient-history association with sleep-related falling, with no dried fig exposure or episode-rate comparison.

fit: symptom measurement review and cited network findings
assessment: The complete review discusses visual symptom classification, limitations of general hallucination rating instruments, visual processing, REM intrusion and the proposed interaction of resting-state and attention networks. Its network discussion revisits cited group findings. It supplies no oral fig comparison or estimate of visual episode frequency after dietary exposure.

fit: case observations in wet macular degeneration and a separate retinal experiment
assessment: Five people with advanced wet macular degeneration reported newly apparent or enhanced light-dependent patterned hallucinations during prescribed proton pump inhibitor exposure. The clinical cases had no Parkinson history. A separate retinal experiment addressed a possible mechanism for those drugs, with no dried fig exposure.

fit: experimental visual effects in healthy volunteers
assessment: Fifteen healthy volunteers were analyzed in a randomized double-blind within-person comparison of pharmacologically induced visual experiences and electrophysiologic measures. Receptor antagonism altered the induced effects in that setting. The study does not test dried fig, typical Parkinson symptoms, or clinical visual episode rates.

fit: Parkinson clinical visual groups and default-mode activity
assessment: Resting-state imaging compared 12 Parkinson participants with complex visual hallucinations, 12 without and 14 controls. Parkinson groups showed altered default-mode connectivity, with higher connectivity in the hallucination group than the nonhallucination group in the reported contrast. Grouping by established symptoms does not measure an exposure response.

fit: Parkinson visual outcomes and hippocampal MRI
assessment: Multimodal hippocampal MRI compared 12 Parkinson participants with visual hallucinations, 15 without and 14 controls. The hallucination group showed microstructural and connectivity differences, with no overall hippocampal volume or shape difference. It includes visual symptom characterization and visuospatial testing, with no dried fig-related outcome.

fit: human fig preparation trial with different population and bowel endpoints
assessment: Controlled oral Ficus carica paste in 80 young adults with functional constipation compared with placebo for eight weeks. The paper excludes neurological disorders. Colon transit, stool form and abdominal discomfort favored the paste. Between-group weekly bowel movement frequency and pain remained inconclusive. The paste and gastrointestinal outcomes leave the intact dried fig and Parkinson visual outcome untested. PMID27440682 and NCT02138851 identify the same result family. NCT01185431 lacks posted results.
